reflections.summary: Lost primarily because the chosen Trick Room mode could not convert its early advantage: Mega Gengar repeatedly used Protect and Taunt while Excadrill applied decisive Ground pressure, leaving Farigiraf and both slow attackers unable to sustain momentum. Armortail and Sneasler's early pressure removed Tyranitar and Tauros, but Sneasler could not threaten Gengar, and the opposing Protect cycles denied key attacks. No between-game adjustment is evidenced, so its effect cannot be credited or blamed; the game-2 plan itself ultimately backfired against Gengar plus Excadrill. The four brought were serviceable but not ideal: Farigiraf was valuable for Trick Room and Armortail, while Armarouge's Wide Guard and Archaludon's Snarl were relevant options, but the composition lacked a reliable Gengar answer and was highly vulnerable to Excadrill. No Mega Stone holder was evolved, and no supplied evidence shows that any registered Pokémon had a Mega Stone. The registered six had useful anti-priority and spread-control tools, but their sets did not adequately cover Taunt, Protect stalling, Ghost immunity interactions, and Ground pressure. The four omitted Pokémon might have offered a better alternative, but their sets are not supplied, so a materially superior replacement cannot be established.
reflections.adjustment: For a rematch, do not rely on a single slow Trick Room line. Preserve Farigiraf long enough to control Taunt and speed, bring a direct way to pressure or deny Mega Gengar, and avoid spending Sneasler's main attack into Gengar's immunity. Force value through Protect with double-targeting, disruption, or defensive positioning rather than repeatedly attacking into it. Keep Wide Guard available for Excadrill and Tyranitar spread attacks, while respecting Excadrill's Focus Sash and Ground pressure. If the omitted roster has a proven Gengar answer or Ground immunity, test that Pokémon over the least effective member; otherwise retain the core but alter the opening so Gengar cannot freely Taunt and stall Trick Room.
reflections.notebook: Mega Gengar is Timid, uses Protect frequently, carries Taunt and Shadow Ball, and can stall turns while disrupting Trick Room; it was Mega Evolved in this game. Excadrill is Adamant with Focus Sash and Sand Rush, carries High Horsepower, Iron Head, Rock Slide, and Protect, and is the main Ground-pressure partner. Tyranitar provides Sand Stream, Protect, Rock Slide, Crunch, and Helping Hand. Tauros-Paldea-Aqua carries Intimidate, Aqua Jet, Close Combat, Wave Crash, and Protect. Armortail blocks priority such as Aqua Jet, but it does not prevent Taunt. Trick Room teams need a plan for Mega Gengar's Taunt and Protect cycles, plus a Ground-resistant answer to Excadrill. Wide Guard is valuable against this opponent's Rock Slide users, and Archaludon's Snarl can reduce special pressure, but neither solves Gengar's immunity, Taunt, or repeated Protect by itself. Prepare a non-Trick-Room or anti-stall route and do not assume early removal of Tyranitar ends the sand matchup.

reflections.summary: Won game 2 and the series 2-0. The sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill provided strong speed control against the opponent's Trick Room + slow attacker strategy. Mega Gengar's Taunt pressure and Shadow Tag were pivotal, and Excadrill's High Horsepower cleaned up after sand was set. The opponent's Farigiraf used Mental Herb to cure Taunt and still set Trick Room on turn 1, but the team's Protect sequencing and raw damage output overwhelmed the TR window. Tauros contributed Intimidate support but fell early to Psychic Noise after Aqua Jet was blocked by Armor Tail. Excadrill's crit on Armarouge on turn 5 was fortunate but the position was already winning. Gengar finished the weakened Archaludon cleanly. No decision errors were recorded.
reflections.adjustment: The same four (Gengar, Tyranitar, Excadrill, Tauros) were brought for game 2 after winning game 1, and the choice held up well. In a future series, consider whether Gholdengo over Tauros adds value: Gholdengo resists Archaludon's Dragon Pulse and Armarouge's Expanding Force, and provides Make It Rain spread damage. However, Tauros's Intimidate and Ground-type coverage for Archaludon are real assets. The current bring is solid; the main tweak would be better Protect sequencing around Farigiraf's Mental Herb Trick Room, perhaps doubling into Farigiraf on turn 1 instead of splitting Taunt + Protect.
reflections.notebook: Opponent tendencies: favors Trick Room + slow heavy hitters (Archaludon, Armarouge) with Farigiraf as TR setter and Armor Tail priority blocker. Sneasler is the speed threat outside TR; Mega Gengar at 200 Spe outspeeds it. Farigiraf runs Mental Herb, so Taunt alone does not stop TR on the setup turn — expect TR to go up regardless; plan to play under it or stall it out with Protect. Archaludon has Stamina (+1 Def per hit) and Leftovers; physical hits boost its defense, so special attacks (Gengar Shadow Ball) are the cleaner answer. Armarouge runs Charcoal Expanding Force and Wide Guard; under TR it threatens Gengar heavily. Sneasler is Jolly with Fake Out and Close Combat; Gengar's Ghost typing immunizes Close Combat. Opponent left Mamoswine and Dedenne on the bench both games — Mamoswine (Focus Sash, Ice Shard) would threaten Gengar and Excadrill; Dedenne (Nuzzle, Eerie Impulse) would disrupt special attackers. Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) is the strongest answer to this opponent's TR archetype. Mega Gengar is the correct Mega choice; Shadow Tag prevents switches during TR turns and Taunt limits late-game setup.
